instruments.title: The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (as amended up to the IFSCA Act, 2019)
applies_to: Every person resident in India, and every person resident outside India dealing in foreign exchange, foreign securities or Indian assets covered by the Act
Authorised persons, including authorised dealer banks
key_concepts: Person resident in India and person resident outside India (s. 2(v) and (w))
Dealing in foreign exchange only through an authorised person (s. 3)

Capital account transactions (s. 6): RBI specifies permissible debt instruments transactions (s. 6(2)); the Central Government covers non-debt instruments (s. 6(2A)) and decides what is a debt instrument (s. 6(7))
Duties of authorised persons (s. 10)
Directions to authorised persons (s. 11)
Penalties (s. 13) and enforcement of orders (ss. 14 and 14A)
Compounding (s. 15)
Adjudication and appeals (ss. 16 to 19 and 35)
Contravention by companies (s. 42)
core_obligations: s. 3: no person may deal in or transfer foreign exchange or foreign security, or make any payment to or receive any payment from a person resident outside India, except as the Act, rules or regulations allow or with general or special permission of RBI
s. 6(3): RBI may by regulations prohibit, restrict or regulate borrowing or lending in foreign exchange and in rupees between residents and non-residents, and the giving of guarantees

s. 10(5): an authorised person must, before carrying out a transaction, require the customer to make such declaration and give such information as reasonably satisfies it that the transaction will not contravene the Act
s. 10(4) and 11: authorised persons must comply with RBI's directions and furnish the information RBI calls for
timelines: s. 14: civil imprisonment may follow if a penalty is not paid within 90 days of the notice to pay
s. 15(1): compounding within 180 days of the application
s. 16(6): the adjudicating authority tries to dispose of a complaint within one year
s. 17 and 19: appeal within 45 days of receiving the order (the Tribunal may require the penalty to be deposited first)
s. 35: appeal to the High Court on a question of law within 60 days, extendable by another 60 days
consequences_stated: s. 11(3): an authorised person that breaches RBI directions or fails to file a return may be fined up to Rs 10,000, and up to Rs 2,000 a day for a continuing breach
s. 13(1): up to three times the sum involved, or up to Rs 2 lakh where the amount cannot be quantified, plus up to Rs 5,000 a day while the contravention continues

s. 13(1A) to (1C): for foreign exchange, foreign security or immovable property held abroad above the notified threshold (s. 37A), up to three times the sum, confiscation of an equivalent value in India, and imprisonment of up to five years
s. 42: every person in charge of and responsible to the company for its business, and any director, manager, secretary or officer whose consent, connivance or neglect is shown, is deemed guilty
instruments.consequences_general: Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999: a person who contravenes the Act, or any rule, regulation, notification, direction or order under it, is liable to a penalty of up to three times the sum involved where it can be quantified, or up to Rs 2 lakh where it cannot, and a further penalty of up to Rs 5,000 a day while the contravention continues (s. 13(1)). The adjudicating authority may also order confiscation of the currency, security or property involved (s. 13(2)). A penalty not paid within 90 days of the notice to pay can lead to civil imprisonment (s. 14). A contravention may be compounded by RBI or the Directorate of Enforcement within 180 days of the application (s. 15), subject to the exclusions in the Compounding Rules. Every officer in charge of a company's business when it contravened is also liable unless they show lack of knowledge or due diligence (s. 42). Appeals lie to the Special Director (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal within 45 days (ss. 17 and 19), and to the High Court on a question of law within 60 days (s. 35).

instruments.title: Foreign Exchange (Compounding Proceedings) Rules, 2024
applies_to: Any person who has contravened FEMA (other than s. 3(a)) and applies to compound the contravention
key_concepts: Compounding authority in RBI set by the sum involved
Directorate of Enforcement compounds s. 3(a) contraventions
Application fee and the compounding order
Contraventions that cannot be compounded (rule 9)
core_obligations: rule 4(1): RBI officers compound by the sum involved: up to Rs 60 lakh by an Assistant General Manager, up to Rs 2.5 crore by a Deputy General Manager, up to Rs 5 crore by a General Manager, and above Rs 5 crore by a Chief General Manager
rule 4(4): application to RBI's Foreign Exchange Department in the prescribed form with a fee of Rs 10,000 plus applicable GST; contraventions of s. 3(a) go to the Directorate of Enforcement (rule 5)

rule 9: no compounding where the amount involved cannot be quantified, where s. 37A applies, where the Directorate of Enforcement considers it a serious contravention suspected of money-laundering, terror financing or affecting sovereignty, where a penalty has already been imposed under s. 13, or where it needs further investigation
rule 4(2): a contravention cannot be compounded within three years of an earlier similar contravention being compounded
timelines: rule 8: the compounding order is passed within 180 days of the application
rules 10 and 11: the compounding amount is paid within 15 days of the order, failing which the application is treated as never made and the contravention is dealt with under the Act
consequences_stated: If the sum is not paid on time, the compounding fails and adjudication under s. 16 can follow

instruments.title: Master Direction – Compounding of Contraventions under FEMA, 1999 (dated 22-04-2025, updated 23-10-2026)
applies_to: Persons applying to RBI to compound FEMA contraventions, and the RBI offices that handle them
key_concepts: Computation matrix by type of contravention and sum involved
Applications through PRAVAAH
Which RBI office compounds which contravention
Publication of compounding orders
core_obligations: Reporting contraventions (including under the Borrowing and Lending Regulations): Rs 10,000 fixed plus an amount for each year of delay that rises with the sum involved: Rs 1,000 a year below Rs 10 lakh, Rs 2,500 for Rs 10-40 lakh, Rs 7,000 for Rs 40 lakh-1 crore, Rs 50,000 for Rs 1-10 crore, Rs 1 lakh for Rs 10-100 crore and Rs 2 lakh for Rs 100 crore and above
Guarantee contraventions other than reporting: Rs 5 lakh plus 0.050% to 0.075% of the sum per year, trebled where the loan proceeds were brought back into India
Other contraventions: Rs 50,000 plus 0.50% to 0.75% of the sum per year
The compounding amount cannot exceed 300% of the sum involved; for sums below Rs 1 lakh it is capped at simple interest of 5% a year (reporting) or 10% a year (others)
Applications are filed online on PRAVAAH with the Rs 10,000 fee
timelines: Compounding orders are passed within 180 days of a complete application and the amount is paid within 15 days

applies_to: Applicants compounding contraventions of the Borrowing and Lending Regulations, the Guarantees Regulations or the overseas investment framework
key_concepts: Borrowing and lending and guarantee contraventions go to the Regional Office with jurisdiction over the registered office
Overseas investment cases go to one of seven Regional Offices by the prefix of the unique identification number
Mixed cases stay with the Central Office (CEFA, Mumbai)
core_obligations: File compounding applications for contraventions of the Borrowing and Lending Regulations and the Guarantees Regulations with the RBI Regional Office under whose jurisdiction the applicant's registered office falls

instruments.title: Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending) Regulations, 2018 (amended up to 16-02-2026)
applies_to: Persons resident in India borrowing or lending in foreign exchange, or borrowing in rupees from, or lending in rupees to, persons resident outside India
Authorised dealer banks, NBFCs and housing finance institutions lending to non-residents
key_concepts: General prohibition with listed exceptions (regulation 3)
Restricted end-uses for all borrowed funds (regulation 3A)
Foreign currency borrowing, including ECB and trade credit (regulation 4)
Foreign currency lending, including lending abroad (regulation 5)
Rupee borrowing from non-residents (regulation 6)
Rupee lending to non-residents (regulation 7)
Repo by non-residents (regulation 7A)
Change of residential status (regulation 8)
Schedule I: ECB framework; Schedule II: trade credit; Schedule III: lending in foreign currency
core_obligations: regulation 3: no resident may borrow or lend in foreign exchange, or borrow rupees from or lend rupees to a non-resident, except as the regulations allow or with RBI permission

regulation 3A: borrowed funds may not be used for chit funds, Nidhi companies, real estate business or farmhouses, agriculture and plantations (with listed exceptions), trading in transferable development rights, transacting in securities (except strategic corporate actions under company law, the SEBI takeover code, SARFAESI or the IBC), repaying a domestic rupee loan taken for a restricted end-use or classified as NPA, or on-lending for any of these

regulation 3A: borrowing for a construction-development project allows plots to be sold only after trunk infrastructure is developed; an industrial park needs at least 10 units, no unit above 50% and at least 66% of the allocable area for industry
regulation 4B(v) and (vi): a resident individual may borrow up to USD 250,000 from relatives abroad, and a student abroad may borrow up to USD 250,000 for fees and maintenance

regulation 6B(vi): a resident individual may borrow rupees from an NRI or OCI relative on a non-repatriation basis, received by inward remittance or from the lender's NRE, NRO, FCNR(B) or SNRR account; repayment goes only to the lender's NRO account

regulation 7B(i): a registered NBFC or housing finance institution may give a housing loan or vehicle loan to an NRI or OCI cardholder on RBI's terms, and the borrower must not use the money for a restricted end-use
regulation 7B(ii): a resident entity may lend rupees to its NRI or OCI employees under its staff welfare scheme
regulation 7B(iii): a resident individual may lend rupees to an NRI or OCI relative within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme limit
regulation 7A(iv): an AD bank may lend rupees to residents of Bhutan, Nepal and Sri Lanka, and to banks there, for cross-border trade
timelines: Schedule I para 16: Form ECB 1 to get a Loan Registration Number before drawdown; Revised Form ECB 1 and Form ECB 2 within 7 calendar days of the end of the month concerned
consequences_stated: Schedule I para 16(2): a borrower who misses a reporting timeline may pay a late submission fee after completing the reporting
instruments.consequences_general: Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999: a person who contravenes the Act, or any rule, regulation, notification, direction or order under it, is liable to a penalty of up to three times the sum involved where it can be quantified, or up to Rs 2 lakh where it cannot, and a further penalty of up to Rs 5,000 a day while the contravention continues (s. 13(1)). instruments.title: Foreign Exchange Management (Borrowing and Lending) (First Amendment) Regulations, 2026
instruments.status: In force (published in the Gazette on 16-02-2026)
applies_to: Any non-individual resident incorporated or registered under a Central or State Act that may borrow under that Act
Non-resident lenders, foreign branches of RBI-regulated lenders and financial institutions in IFSC
Designated AD Category-I banks
key_concepts: One ECB framework replacing the old tracks, eligible-borrower lists and recognised-lender rules
Borrowing limit: higher of USD 1 billion outstanding or 300% of net worth
Minimum average maturity of 3 years (1-3 years for manufacturers up to USD 150 million)
Market-based cost, with the trade credit ceiling for maturities under 3 years
New end-use list in regulation 3A
New Forms ECB 1 and ECB 2
core_obligations: Schedule I para 1: entities under restructuring or insolvency resolution may borrow only if the approved plan allows it; an entity facing a FEMA investigation, adjudication or appeal may borrow but must disclose it in Form ECB 1
Schedule I para 2: an ECB may be raised from any person resident outside India, a foreign branch of an RBI-regulated lender, or a financial institution in IFSC
Schedule I para 3: the ECB may be in foreign currency or rupees, and the currency may be changed in any direction at an exchange rate that does not raise the liability

Schedule I para 4: any commercial borrowing with interest and principal repayment counts, including FCCBs and FCEBs; preference shares or debentures that are not fully and mandatorily convertible, issued on or after 30-04-2007, are ECB; trade credit up to 3 years, export advances, Debt Instruments Regulations investments, convertible notes and FVCI debt are not

Schedule I para 5: ECB up to the higher of USD 1 billion outstanding or total borrowing of 300% of net worth on the last audited standalone balance sheet; the limit does not apply to entities regulated by a financial sector regulator

Schedule I para 6: minimum average maturity of 3 years; manufacturers may borrow at 1-3 years up to USD 150 million outstanding; no call or put option before the minimum maturity, with exceptions for conversion, repayment from fresh equity, refinance, waiver and corporate actions
Schedule I para 7 to 9: cost in line with market conditions (below 3 years, within the trade credit ceiling); prepayment and penal charges at market terms; related-party ECB at arm's length

Schedule I para 10: drawdown only after the Loan Registration Number; rupee proceeds credited to the designated AD bank by the end of the following month and, pending use, kept in an unencumbered fixed deposit of up to one year

Schedule I para 11: security by charge on assets or by guarantee under the Guarantees Regulations 2026, with a security clause in the loan agreement and a no-objection certificate from existing lenders; entities regulated by RBI shall not issue any guarantee

Schedule I para 13: conversion of ECB, including matured unpaid ECB, into equity under the NDI Rules with no extra cost, with lender consent and subject to RBI's restructuring norms where the borrower has RBI-regulated lenders
ECBs with a Loan Registration Number obtained before the amendment continue on their earlier terms, except for reporting
timelines: Revised Form ECB 1 within 7 calendar days of the end of the month in which a change takes effect
Form ECB 2 within 7 calendar days of the end of the month of drawdown or debt servicing

Appeals lie to the Special Director (Appeals) or the Appellate Tribunal within 45 days (ss. 17 and 19), and to the High Court on a question of law within 60 days (s. 35).

instruments.short_name: ECB and Trade Credit Master Direction
instruments.title: Master Direction – External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations (updated 08-09-2026)
instruments.status: In force (ECB part now in the Regulations; trade credit part continues)
applies_to: Resident importers raising trade credit
AD Category-I banks handling ECB and trade credit
key_concepts: Trade credit framework (para 14)
Trade credit in SEZ and FTWZ (para 15)
Security for trade credit (para 16)
Monthly Form TC (para 17)
Role of AD banks (para 18)
The ECB paragraphs (1 to 12) were deleted on 16-02-2026 when the framework moved into the Regulations
core_obligations: para 14: trade credit up to USD 150 million per import transaction for oil and gas refining and marketing companies, airlines and shipping companies, and USD 50 million for others

para 14: lenders are the supplier (suppliers' credit) or banks, financial institutions, foreign equity holders and IFSC financial institutions (buyers' credit); foreign branches of Indian banks may give only foreign currency trade credit
para 14: capital goods up to 3 years; non-capital goods up to one year or the operating cycle, whichever is less (shipyards up to 3 years)
para 14: all-in-cost ceiling of benchmark plus 300 bps for new foreign currency trade credit, and benchmark plus 250 bps for rupee trade credit

para 16.1: AD banks may issue guarantees to the overseas lender up to the trade credit amount and for no longer than the permitted period; letters of undertaking and letters of comfort are not permitted
para 16.2: the importer may offer a charge on movable or immovable assets (not land in SEZs) or a corporate or personal guarantee, with the AD bank's oversight
timelines: para 17.1: AD banks file a monthly consolidated Form TC by the 10th of the following month

instruments.short_name: Rupee borrowing and lending with NRIs
instruments.title: Master Direction – Borrowing and Lending transactions in Indian Rupee between Persons Resident in India and Non-Resident Indians / Persons of Indian Origin (updated 08-09-2026)
instruments.theme: Rupee borrowing and lending with non-residents
applies_to: AD banks, registered NBFCs and housing finance institutions lending rupees to NRIs or persons of Indian origin
Resident individuals and bodies corporate lending to NRI relatives or employees
key_concepts: AD bank loans to NRIs against security (para 3)
Housing loans to NRIs and PIOs (para 4)
Staff loans (para 5)
Loans by resident individuals to NRI relatives (para 6)
Change of residential status (para 7)
core_obligations: para 3.1: AD banks may lend rupees to NRIs against shares, securities or immovable property; the loan may not be remitted abroad or credited to the borrower's NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR account
para 3.2: loans to NRI employees to buy ESOP shares are limited to 90% of the purchase price or Rs 20 lakh per employee, whichever is lower

para 4: AD banks and housing finance institutions approved by NHB may give housing loans to NRIs and PIOs on the terms that apply to residents; the loan is not credited to NRE or FCNR(B) accounts, and repayment comes by inward remittance, from the borrower's NRE, FCNR(B) or NRO account, from rent on the property, or by a relative in India

para 5: a body corporate in India may lend rupees to its NRI or PIO employees for personal purposes, including housing, under its staff welfare scheme; the loan is credited to the borrower's NRO account and repaid only by remittance or from the borrower's NRE, NRO or FCNR(B) account

para 6: a resident individual may lend an NRI relative an interest-free loan of at least one year by crossed cheque or electronic transfer, within the LRS limit, credited to the borrower's NRO account and not remitted abroad

instruments.title: Foreign Exchange Management (Guarantees) Regulations, 2026
applies_to: Any person resident in India who is a surety, principal debtor or creditor in a guarantee where any other party is resident outside India
AD banks issuing guarantees backed by non-resident counter-guarantees or collateral
key_concepts: Single prohibition with permitted cases
Surety and principal debtor must each be eligible to lend and borrow under the Borrowing and Lending Regulations
Reporting of issue, change and invocation
Late submission fee
core_obligations: regulation 3: no resident may be a party to a guarantee where any other party is resident outside India, except as these regulations allow
regulation 4: the regulations do not apply to guarantees by AD bank branches outside India or in IFSC, by custodians for IPCs, or guarantees under the Overseas Investment Regulations

regulation 5: a resident may be a surety or principal debtor if the underlying transaction is permitted under FEMA and both the surety and the principal debtor are eligible to lend and borrow under the Borrowing and Lending Regulations
regulation 5: AD banks may also issue guarantees backed by a counter-guarantee or 100% collateral from a non-resident, and guarantees for shipping or airline agents
regulation 6: a resident may be the creditor in a guarantee given by a non-resident surety where the underlying transaction is permitted
regulation 7: the resident surety reports the guarantee (or, if there is none, the resident principal debtor, or else the resident creditor) through the AD bank
timelines: regulation 7: issue, change and invocation reported to the AD bank within 15 days of the end of the quarter
regulation 7: the AD bank reports to RBI within 30 days of the end of the quarter
consequences_stated: regulation 8: late reporting may be regularised by a late submission fee of Rs 7,500 plus 0.025% of the amount involved for each year of delay
